summary.en: Success came harder for the Rolling Stones than for the Beatles.
summary.zh: The Rolling Stones的成功比The Beatles来得要更难一些。

body.zh:
当我们提到The Rolling Stones在美国的经历，回看往期榜单，首先意识到与The Beatles相比，The Rolling Stones在美国的立足过程更为艰辛。在The Beatles的故事中我们说过，1964年2月9日他们在The Ed Sullivan Show登台表演，突然间名声大噪，很多歌曲同时上榜，他们曾同时占据单曲榜前5的位置，这是多么大的成就。不仅在美国，在全世界也是如此。

The Rolling Stones一开始并非如此，他们在纽约或洛杉矶这样的大城市巡演，观众还是很多的。但当他们走到美国中部进行拼盘演出，就没有那么多观众了。他们必须更努力地争取机会，最终他们取得了空前成功，并且能到世界上任何想演出的地方演出，体育场内座无虚席，但这一切对The Rolling Stones来说来得有点慢。

有趣的是，他们的经纪人Andrew Loog Oldham最开始建议他们包装成与The Beatles相反的形象，The Stones应该做坏小子。因为The Beatles已经建立起了好男孩形象，他们有魅力、阳光、诙谐、又吸引人。对于美国父母来说，自己女儿和这样的男孩交往，应该不会反对。而The Rolling Stones则是父母极力反对自己女儿交往的对象，他们吸烟、酗酒、外表邋遢，看起来放荡不羁，无疑是坏小子。有趣的是，我们可以看到这种好男孩和坏小子的市场策略在流行乐坛中反复出现。比如1956到1958年期间，Pat Bonne就是好男孩，Elvis就是坏小子。事实上，Elvis去军队服役一定程度就是为了扭转自己的坏小子形象，以便更多地进入主流流行乐圈。1960到1963年间Elvis演了些电影，他在电影里要多乖有多乖。同样的，在这里The Rolling Stones代表的是坏孩子形象，而The Beatles则是好男孩。

The Rolling Stones没有马上成功，但是1965年他们的热门歌曲《(I Can't Get No) Satisfaction》在英美两地都拿到了第一，使他们成为明星。有人说这首歌的歌词讲述了他们遭遇的性挫折，像歌词I Can't Get No Satisfaction说的那样。其实这首歌讲了他们在人生各方面的不满意，只有一句歌词可以被视为跟性相关。我记得在不久前，63年或者64年，所有人都在找歌里可能蕴含的冒犯的话。拿《Louie Louie》为例，FBI曾经介入调查这盘磁带，用了各种先进设备来检测歌里是否带有下流词句，最后的结论是，他们不能确定。不管怎样，歌里一个脏词都能让它从播放列表上消失。但The Rolling Stones根本不打算否认歌里对于性不满的表达，这就巩固了他们的坏小子形象，但这歌又没有明目张胆到要被禁掉的程度。这是一个非常出色的推广，将他们归为英伦入侵中游手好闲的那一类。

其他在65、66年的金曲有：65年英美都拿了第一的《Get Off My Cloud》，66年两国榜单第一的《Paint It Black》，还有其他一些成绩不错的歌曲。

可能很多The Rolling Stones的粉丝持有不同观点，但我的观点是：20世纪60年代，The Rolling Stones处在The Beatles的阴影之下，63、64年的时候，The Rolling Stones还是The Bealtes的小弟，The Beatles的成就盖过了The Rolling Stones，很多情况下The Rolling Stones只是在模仿The Beatles先前的表演，该情况持续到1969年《Abbey Road》发布后，The Beatles举步维艰面临解散。

当The Beatles解散后，The Rolling Stones好像放下了重担，70年代初，他们开始绽放异彩，用70年代的摇滚回归本我。来想想一些歌，比如《Sticky Fingers》这张专辑，从此开始，The Rolling Stones才变成了真正的自己。回顾The Rolling Stones的成功，在他们如此闪耀之后回过头来看，我们可能会不自觉夸大他们最初的水准。他们是伟大的，但可能The Beatles总是更伟大一些。再次说明，关于这个问题有很多看法或解释。接下来我们继续谈谈英伦入侵中的其他英国乐队，以及他们的音乐风格
body.en:
When we talk about the Rolling Stones in America and look back at the charts, the first thing to notice is that their foothold was harder than the Beatles’. In the Beatles story we said that on 9 February 1964 they appeared on the Ed Sullivan Show and suddenly exploded—many songs charting at once; they once held the top five singles slots. That is enormous—not only in America but worldwide.

The Stones were not like that at first. In big cities like New York or Los Angeles, audiences were still large. But on package tours through the American Midwest, crowds thinned. They had to work harder for opportunities. Eventually they had unprecedented success and could play anywhere they wanted to packed stadiums—but for the Stones that came a bit slowly.

Interestingly, manager Andrew Loog Oldham first advised packaging them as the opposite of the Beatles: the Stones should be the bad boys. The Beatles had built a good-boy image—charming, sunny, witty, appealing. American parents would not mind their daughters dating such boys. The Stones were whom parents forbade—smoking, drinking, scruffy, seeming dissolute: bad boys for sure. Amusingly, this good-boy / bad-boy market strategy recurs in pop. From 1956 to 1958 Pat Boone was the good boy, Elvis the bad boy. In fact Elvis’s army service was partly to soften the bad-boy image and enter mainstream pop more fully. From 1960 to 1963 Elvis made films in which he was as well-behaved as could be. Here the Stones stand for the bad kids, the Beatles for the good boys.

The Stones did not succeed at once, but in 1965 “(I Can’t Get No) Satisfaction” hit No. 1 in Britain and America and made them stars. Some say the lyrics are about sexual frustration—as “I Can’t Get No Satisfaction” suggests. Actually the song is about dissatisfaction in many areas of life; only one line can be read as sexual. I recall that not long before—’63 or ’64—everyone hunted for possible offense in songs. Take “Louie Louie”: the FBI once investigated the tape with advanced gear to find dirty words and concluded they could not be sure. Anyway, one dirty word could kill a playlist slot. The Stones did not bother denying sexual dissatisfaction in the song; that solidified the bad-boy image, yet it was not blatant enough to get banned. Excellent promotion—slotting them as the layabout wing of the British Invasion.

Other 1965–66 hits: “Get Off of My Cloud,” No. 1 in both countries in 1965; “Paint It Black,” No. 1 in both in 1966; plus other strong charting songs.

Many Stones fans may disagree, but my view is: in the 1960s the Stones stood in the Beatles’ shadow. In 1963–64 they were still the Beatles’ little brothers; Beatles achievements overshadowed them, and often the Stones were imitating what the Beatles had already done—until after Abbey Road in 1969, when the Beatles struggled toward breakup.

After the Beatles broke up, the Stones seemed to drop a heavy load. In the early 1970s they bloomed, returning to themselves with 1970s rock. Think of albums like Sticky Fingers—from then on the Stones became truly themselves. Looking back at their success after they shone so brightly, we may unconsciously inflate how strong they were at the start. They were great—but perhaps the Beatles were always a bit greater. Again, many views and explanations exist. Next we continue with other British Invasion bands and their styles.
